episodes.194454: An upper level low and jet streak forced unusually strong shear over the region, which|managed to generate some strong storms. A few storms become severe.
episodes.194513: As the remains of Tropical System Francine slowly meandered through the mid South, a persistent band of showers and thunderstorms produced very heavy rainfall totals over the two day period from the 13th into the 14th.  Some of the heaviest rains occurred during the evening of the 13th into the morning hours of the 14th in parts of northwest and north central Alabama. Widespread rain totals of 2 to 4 inches were observed, with a large pocket of 4 to 6 inch rainfall across portions of Cullman, Colbert, Franklin, Lauderdale, Lawrence, and Morgan.  A smaller pocket of 8 to 12 inch rainfall was observed in Lawrence Cunty, including the Bankhead National Forest.  During the evening hours of the 13th, a few instances of flash flooding weres reported in Cullman County. During the late night and morning hours of the 14th, significant flash and areal flooding occurred as a result in the town of Moulton and nearby areas where several homes were affected by flood water.  Small stream and creek flooding persisted through the 15th as runoff fed into the Big Nance Creek which went into Major Flood during the morning hours.  A man was rescued from flood waters during the early morning hours of the 15th just south of Courtland near a creek feeding into Big Nance Creek.
episodes.194597: Hurricane Francine made landfall along the Louisiana coast during the afternoon of September 11. Downgraded to a tropical depression as it moved northward through Mississippi the next day, Francine brought gradient wind gusts of 30-40 mph to Central Alabama. Numerous trees were downed across several counties, with some falling on power lines and across roadways. One minor injury occurred in Jefferson County when a tree fell onto a passing pickup truck.||The next couple days brought bands of heavy rainfall and gusty winds to the area as activity became increasing associated with a nearly stationary surface boundary. One storm in Blount County on the 13th produced hail over quarter-size, with another storm shortly after causing an area of tree and minor structural damage near Locust Fork. Heavy rainfall caused flooding issues in Birmingham the morning of the 14th, in Eufaula around midday on the 14th, and in Birmingham again just after midnight on the 15th.
episodes.194627: Several showers and thunderstorms developed in association with the remnants of Hurricane Francine and a stalled frontal boundary.  Several areas of rotation were detected, but no tornado touchdowns were reported.  There was one report of a tree down in Walton county.  In addition, heavy rainfall led to areas of flash flooding.
episodes.194934: A thunderstorm became severe south of Rapid City and moved east-northeast into eastern Pennington County. The storm produced wind gusts to over 60 mph along its path.
episodes.195835: A thunderstorm produced a strong wind gust in the Indian River near Grant.
episodes.195936: A strong area of low pressure caused wide spread coastal and riverine flooding across the lower Kuskokwim Valley.  The gale force winds enhanced high tides and backed up flow from the Kuskokwim River, flooding numerous communities along the river.  High tide combined with the high winds from the low exacerbated high water across the region with water flowing into communities along the river.
episodes.195998: A coastal trough off the Carolina coast was the focus for shower and thunderstorm activity throughout much of the day on September 13th. Ongoing shower and thunderstorm activity along the Crystal Coast and points offshore gradually shifted to the north as the day went on. A few of these storms became strong to severe in nature bringing damaging wind gusts to portions of the Crystal Coast during the afternoon.
episodes.196279: A continued moist airmass and weak storm motion produced diurnally enhanced showers and isolated storms with localized flooding.
episodes.196394: Breezy winds and 1-2 inches of rainfall occurred in Western Kentucky from the remnants of Hurricane Francine. Thunderstorm activity was limited, though a small group of thunderstorms developed in an outer rainband moving northwestward late afternoon. One stronger downdraft from these storms damaged a carport in Cerulean Springs. Strong moisture convergence was present with these storms, though rainfall duration was limited, keeping rainfall totals in Western Kentucky from Francine remnants around 1-2 inches.
episodes.196413: A cold front moved into western North Dakota, which led to thunderstorm development during the evening hours. Some of the storms became severe, producing damaging wind gusts. The strongest wind gusts, which occurred in Hettinger County north of Burt, were estimated at 80 mph. These wind gusts caused significant damage to a pole barn roof, calf shelter, wind break panels, and a water tank.
episodes.196596: A couple of bands of strong to severe thunderstorms developed during the afternoon and persisted into the nighttime in north central Alabama.  These occurred as the remnants of Francine shifted west in Arkansas, and instability increased over Alabama within the dry slot.
episodes.196663: Another tropical wave moved into the region by the middle of September. With previously saturated soils, and additional showers and thunderstorms, mudslides, gusty winds and flooding was reported in Puerto Rico. This event brought rainfall accumulations of 1 to 2 inches per day, especially in the interior and west, and portions of eastern Puerto Rico, including the San Juan metro area.
episodes.196920: High atmospheric moisture levels across South Florida, sea breeze convergence, and storm motion from west to east, resulted in showers and thunderstorms affecting the SE Florida coast during the late afternoon and evening hours.
episodes.197026: Several showers and thunderstorms moved in a training motion over portions of west and central Georgia over the course of the day on September 13, 2024. With mid-level energy and ample moisture from the remnants of Hurricane Francine, stronger storms became efficient rainfall producers and led to localized flash flooding.
episodes.197033: TS Bebinca originated in the Federated States of Micronesia near Pohnpei and Kosrae as a surface trough. Bebinca gradually consolidated into a closed low-level circulation as it moved WNW past Pohnpei and Chuuk as was monitored as Invest 95W. The Joint Typhoon Warning Center (JTWC) issued its first warning on TD 14W as it sat about 200 miles SE of Guam on 10 Sep. It was briefly elevated to a 40 mph TS as it passed to the west of southern Guam early morning on the 11th. Rainfall was the more notable hazard with Guam seeing the bulk of rainfall. Heavy rains were less prevalent across the CNMI, but Saipan did see some erosion and runoff due to all the loose soil and gravel from large stretches of road work. Little wind damage was reported beyond some downed limbs and fleshier vegetations such as banana and papaya trees.

events.narrative: The GW0525 Bloomfield mesonet station (G0525) measured a 58 mph thunderstorm wind gust.
A significant portion of a pole barn roof was lifted and folded back. A calf shelter was destroyed, wind bread panels were scattered, and a one-thousand gallon water tank blew over and rolled.
Wind gusts were estimated at near 60 mph.

After the passage of TS Bebinca, a south-southwest monsoon pattern setup across the Marianas. An intense cluster of heavy showers and thunderstorms moved across Guam from Barrigada and up to Andersen Air Force Base (central to northern Guam) from about 1500ChST to 1600ChST on December 13th, just a couple of days after Bebinca developed just west of Guam and brought several inches of rain, so much of Guam was already saturated. The weather office recorded 2.4 inches within that one hour timeframe, with radar estimates of  2 to 4 inches across the area. Several reports of cars stalling on flooded roads with sections of the roads becoming impassable, such as the north and south bound outer lanes of  Route (Highway) 1 near Carlos Heights upper Tumon. Similar flooding was seen by a NWS employee on the low-lying section of Route (Highway) 8, which is located near the weather office. No official damage estimate was given, but a rough estimate of flood damage to stalled cars is estimated to be around 2.5 Thousand $USD.

National Weather Service Birmingham meteorologists surveyed storm damage in and near the Locust Fork area of Blount County on Saturday, September 14. The survey team found a broad area impacted by damaging winds generally across portions of Blount County west of Locust Fork. Damage surveyors found widespread small tree limb damage with a few large tree limbs down and a couple of uprooted trees sporadically through the wind damage area. There was no signature of convergence or divergence observed in the wind damage pattern, indicative of straight line winds. The majority of the area appeared to experience damaging winds from 40-50 mph with a pocket of higher winds from 50-60 mph. Much of the structural damage observed in the area appeared to be the result of falling tree limbs or tree limbs falling onto power lines, although some smaller sheds were flipped or demolished.

The public reported that their driveway had ruts 12 inches deep from running water through town down to the bay.  You could hear the water running through town down to the bay from the end of Ave C Road.
